lines.text: Open a website, and sometimes you stare at a blank white screen.
Then a spinner. Then, finally, the content.
Other sites simply appear, instantly.
The difference is where the page gets built: in the browser, or on a server.
Today: [CSR|client side rendering], [SSR|server side rendering], and [RSC|React Server Components].
With diagrams, animations, and real code we actually ran.
Every page involves three players: the browser, the server, and a database.
Rendering means turning components and data into [HTML|H T M L] that the browser can paint.
So who does the rendering? The browser, or the server?
Think of buying a bookshelf.
[CSR|Client side rendering] is flat-pack. A box of parts arrives, and you build it at home.
[SSR|Server side rendering] is pre-built. It arrives ready, but there is a catch, which we will meet soon.
Let's start with [CSR|client side rendering], the classic React app.
Step one: the browser asks for the page.
The server replies with an almost empty [HTML|H T M L] file: one empty div, and a script tag.
Step two: the browser downloads the JavaScript bundle, with React and all your components.
Step three: React runs, and builds the page inside that empty div.
Step four: the component asks an [API|A P I] for its data, and only then can it draw the real content.
Until then, the user sees a blank screen, or a spinner.
In code, the shell is tiny: a root div, and one script.
Then [createRoot|create root] takes over that div.
The data is fetched inside [useEffect|use effect], after the first render.
Two round trips: one for the code, one for the data.
What is good about [CSR|client side rendering]?
Hosting is cheap, because the server only sends static files.
And after the first load, navigating feels fast.
The downsides: first content is late, and the bundle grows with your app.
Also, some crawlers and link previews do not run JavaScript, so they see only an empty div.
Now [SSR|server side rendering]. Here, the server does the building.
It runs your React components, fetches the data close to home, and produces real [HTML|H T M L].
The browser paints that [HTML|H T M L] immediately: the headline, the text, everything.
Here is a real component: a heading, and a counter button.
On the server, [renderToString|render to string] turns it into plain [HTML|H T M L].
The output has the heading, and a button that says clicked zero times.
No JavaScript was needed to see it. Crawlers and slow phones get real content in the very first response.
Now the catch. That [HTML|H T M L] is only a picture of the page.
The button is there, but clicking it does nothing. No event handlers are attached yet.
So the browser also downloads the same JavaScript, and React runs [hydrateRoot|hydrate root].
Hydration walks the existing [HTML|H T M L], matches it to your components, and attaches the event listeners.
It reuses the elements that are already there. It does not rebuild the page.
Now the button is alive.
One warning: server and browser must render the same output, or React reports a hydration mismatch.
Let's race them.
With [CSR|C S R], content appears late, after the code and the data both arrive.
With [SSR|S S R], content appears much earlier.
But there is a gap before hydration finishes, where the page looks ready, and is not.
And [SSR|S S R] needs a running server.
Neither always wins. It is a trade-off.
What if one part of the page is slow, like customer reviews?
Streaming helps. Wrap the slow part in [Suspense|suspense].
React sends the shell right away, with a fallback in the gap.
When the reviews are ready, the server streams them in, and a tiny script swaps them into place.
We ran it: fallback first, reviews later, in the same response.
But [SSR|server side rendering] still has a problem.
Every component ships its JavaScript to the browser, so it can hydrate.
Even the ones that never change, like a footer.
That code is downloaded and run, just to redo work the server already did.
What if components that never need interactivity simply never left the server?
That is the idea behind React Server Components.
A server component runs only on the server. Its code is never sent to the browser.
So it can be async, and read straight from a database.
Here, the product page awaits its data, and renders the name and price.
No [useEffect|use effect], no loading state, no extra [API|A P I] route.
Interactive parts, like a like button, are client components. You mark them with [use client|use client] at the top of the file.
Only those are shipped as JavaScript, and hydrated.
In Next.js, components are server components by default.
So what does the server send? Not [HTML|H T M L], and not JavaScript.
It sends the [RSC|R S C] payload: a compact description of the rendered tree. This is a real one we captured.
The article, the heading, and the price are plain data.
And where the like button goes, there is a placeholder, and a reference to its JavaScript file.
React in the browser fills in the tree, and hydrates only that client piece.
When you navigate, Next.js fetches only the payload, and React updates the page in place.
Two rules about the boundary.
Everything imported by a [use client|use client] file becomes client code too.
A server component can render a client component, but not the other way around.
So keep the boundary low: make only the small interactive leaves client components.
There is also [use server|use server], for server functions that the client can call, like form actions.
Treat them as public endpoints, and always validate and authorize inside them.
Is a server component the same as [SSR|S S R]? No.
[SSR|S S R] makes [HTML|H T M L] for a fast first paint.
Server components decide where code runs, and how much JavaScript ships.
Together, the server turns the payload into [HTML|H T M L]. The browser paints it, then hydrates only the client parts.
So which should you use?
A dashboard behind a login? [CSR|C S R] is fine.
A shop or a blog? Render on the server, so people and crawlers see content quickly.
Pages that never change? Static generation builds them once, ahead of time.
In a modern app, mix them: server components by default, client components for interactivity.
Let's recap.
[CSR|C S R] builds the page in the browser.
[SSR|S S R] sends [HTML|H T M L] first, then hydrates it.
Streaming sends the page in pieces.
Server components keep code on the server, so the browser downloads less.
Thanks for watching.
